questions.q: What is the basic rule for changing a direct speech sentence in present tense to indirect speech when the reporting verb is in past tense?
questions.a: The tense of the reported speech shifts one step back (e.g., present simple becomes past simple). A wrong answer (e.g., "tense doesn't change") reveals the student hasn't grasped the backshifting rule, which is fundamental for indirect speech conversion.

questions.q: In the sentence "fe;k¡ ulh#íhu us iapg”kkjh vank”k ls flj fgyk;k", identify the perception verb and explain how its meaning differs from simple "ns[kuk".
questions.a: The perception verb is "flj fgyk;k" (looked angrily). Unlike "ns[kuk" (neutral seeing), "flj fgyk;k" conveys an emotional attitude (anger) through the adverbial phrase "flj" modifying the act of seeing. A wrong answer that just says "ns[kuk" misses the nuance of perception verbs combined with adverbs to show manner.

questions.q: Compare the word order in these two sentences from the text: (a) "fe;k¡ e'kgwj gSa NIiu fdLe dh jksfV;k¡ cukus osQ fy,A" (b) "fudky ysaxs oDr FkksM+k". Explain why the author might choose the order in (a) over the standard SOV.
questions.a: Sentence (a) uses OSV order (Object-Subject-Verb): "NIiu fdLe dh jksfV;k¡" (object) placed before subject "fe;k¡" to emphasize the purpose. Sentence (b) follows standard SOV: "fudky" (adverb) "ysaxs" (subject) "oDr FkksM+k" (verb). The author uses OSV in (a) to highlight the object (making dolls) as the focus of Fe;k¡'s eagerness. A wrong answer that says both are SOV fails to recognize how word order shifts emphasis in Hindi.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of using indirect speech in the narrative when the author writes: "ckn'kkg lyker us I+kQjek;kµ ^dksbZ ,slh ph”k cukvks tks u vkx ls iosQ] u ikuh ls cusA*". Would direct speech be more powerful here? Justify.
questions.a: Indirect speech here summarizes the teacher's suggestion, maintaining narrative flow without breaking into dialogue. Direct speech would be more powerful if the exact words were crucial for character voice, but the author chooses indirect to convey the gist quickly. A wrong answer that says "direct is always better" ignores narrative pacing and the author's stylistic choice.
